419.history: The hill town of the silver seam keeps the sacred wood of Flidais, where the elder teachers of the druid schools met, and its smiths beat the silver neck-rings that the heads of the seven houses first wore in LE 149, so that a stranger might know a custodian by the collar before a word was said. Beathag nic Ruairidh taught in its grove when Coinneach mac Mhàrtainn came to it with the question he had carried on the roads, and told him the schools wanted a fixed ground where it might be argued whole. From LE 479 the schools kept the wood and walked its bounds each year in a procession open to anyone who would walk with them. Twice in the age Clann Choinnich asked that the coal be burned beyond the handful to smelt the silver here, in LE 1,559 and in LE 1,776, and twice the council refused; the second time by a single turned vote.
419.known_for: the silver collars, the wood of Flidais, and the smelt refused

500.history: The fishing town kept its boats and nets shared among the households of a fellowship, and in the third century of the count King Fearchar mac Lachlainn, old and curious, kept one of its fishermen a full hour answering questions on how the sharing was done. Having lost catch to poor curing, it began in LE 394 to send carts north for Ros fhionn salt, and from then the mining shires ate their salt fish cured with salt carried over Drochaid Ros fhionn.
500.known_for: its fishers' fellowship and its salt fish

197.history: The fishing town took the greatest catch of its memory in LE 1,039 and ran out of salt on the second day. The shed-foreman Ruairidh mac Neacail hung what could not be salted on lines strung the length of the lower town's lanes rather than let it spoil on the strand; the dried fish sold poorly against salted, and from that year the town laid in salt for a catch half again the size of any it had taken.
197.known_for: the year the lanes were hung with fish

212.history: The millers of the northern mill town cut a new gearing for their wheels in LE 1,189, oak toothed against oak, so that one wheel turned two stones where it had turned one. Half the town came to watch it the first winter and went away arguing whether the flour was finer or coarser. Within a generation every mill of consequence in the north had it, and the millers hung a carved model of it over their own door as a boast that grew quieter with every mill that copied it without asking leave.
212.known_for: the gearing that turned two stones

475.history: The coastal town at the mouth of the Abhainn ghorm received the grain barges of Inis mhòr from the second century of the count. Its fishers' sons walked three days to sit the benches at Dùn thais, and one of them, Aonghas mac Nèill, stayed to keep the house's register. In LE 1,369 the fishers of silted Caol ìseal came to it and set up their shrine again stone by stone in the same order, so that it stood as it always had.
475.known_for: the shrine carried whole from Caol ìseal

505.history: The town at the hot springs of the east country was founded in LE 190, and in LE 769 its bath-house was rebuilt below it. Coal-breakers, salt-carriers and shepherds sat in the warm water together without minding whose gallery the others answered to, and the old vein-house scribe Eòghann mac Pheadair was carried there by cart in his last cold season.
505.known_for: the bath-house at the hot springs

365.history: The upland town took in so many families from the failing hill farms after a run of poor seasons in the fourth century of the count that it all but doubled, and in LE 324 its reeve marked out shares of the common grazing for households that had never held a share of it before.

259.history: The shire seat of Baile ruadh quarrelled with Achadh naomh over grazing along a stream that had shifted its bed, and in LE 1,246 the king's council divided the ground along the stream as it then ran. Both shire seats carried home the boundary stones they had brought to argue their claims and set them unused into their own walls, where they stood for the rest of the age pointing at a line the water had already drawn.
259.known_for: the boundary stones set into its walls

405.history: The shire seat of Achadh naomh was the other party to the grazing quarrel with Baile ruadh that the king's council settled along the stream in LE 1,246. Like its neighbour it carried home the stones it had brought and set them into its own walls unused.
405.known_for: the grazing quarrel settled by the stream

191.history: The old harbour town of the south-west coast took the coughing sickness in LE 156, and it reached the reeve's own household. His wife would not let their door be barred against the shared board, holding that a household which eats apart out of fear will go on eating apart after the fear has passed; she lived, and the custom of the shared meal outlasted the sickness in that country.
191.known_for: the shared meal kept through the cough

49.history: The fishing town on the wild strait near Inis thais was founded in LE 739. Its fishers had always kept their boats inside the strait that gave the town its name, never past their own headlands, until in LE 1,389 some of them went out and found a safe lane south to the landing at Cidhe Beag. Slighe-mhara Caol fhiadhaich was not believed at first; within a season or two of its being believed, the older harbours of the south coast followed it one after another.

364.history: The village of Cnoc chaol on the south coast lost two children in LE 724 to a great swell that rose with no storm behind it and ran the drying-racks off the beach. The household of one of the drowned struck itself from its old gallery-claim and took up a claim further from the water, and the vein-house's young scribe Eòghann mac Pheadair entered the removal the next season, cold and plain, as he had been taught.
364.known_for: the wave with no storm behind it

86.history: The harbour on the north coast had been silting longer than any one season could be blamed for, and in LE 1,369 its fishing families gave the last of it up and moved east to Caol bheag, carrying their nets, their smoking-racks and the small shrine from the harbour's edge, stone by stone. The town did not empty; the houses nearest the silted water turned to farming the ground behind them, and within two generations it smelled of turned earth rather than fish and tar.
86.known_for: the harbour given up to the plough

232.history: The old town of the south-west coast near Inis thais took the Stone's second house. When the congregation at Inis thais divided in LE 1,389 over whether the dead might be prayed for by name at Clach, those who said they might built their own house of the Stone here, finished within ten years of the first quarrel, and the two congregations went their own ways, neither troubling the other much and neither giving ground.
232.known_for: the second house of the Stone
